title: Multienzyme Isothermal Rapid Amplification-coupled Lateral Flow Assay for Point-of-Care Cervical Cancer Diagnosis through High-Risk Human Papillomavirus Detection
supervisor: Prof. Dr. Gokul Chandra Biswas
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Cervical cancer is a leading cause of cancer death among women around the globe. HPV vaccination has not been properly introduced yet. Screening of cervical cancer incidences still relies on visual inspection with acetic acid. HPV DNA testing, recommended by the World Health Organization, remains unimplemented in developing country like Bangladesh. Quantitative PCR used in HPV DNA testing requires thermal cyclers, stable electricity, cold-chain reagents, and trained personnel. To mitigate these challenges, this study aimed to develop an equipment-free assay for the simultaneous detection of the E6 oncogene of HPV-16 and HPV-18, thereby confirming the incidence of cervical cancer-associated.

The test or diagnosis combines the Multienzyme Isothermal Rapid Amplification (MIRA) of target biomarker with a duplex lateral flow dipstick (LFD). Genotype-specific primers and internal NFO probes were designed against synthetic E6 fragments. An initial design placed fluorescein and hapten labels directly on the primers. This produced false positives outcomes in no-template controls, caused by dual-labelled primer-dimers. The assay was redesigned around an unlabeled forward primer and an internal FAM-labelled NFO probe. Thus, false-positive results were eliminated in negative controls.

Band intensities were quantified by image analysis across reaction temperature, incubation time, and template copy numbers. At 37 °C, which resembles body temperature, both genotypes were detected within 30 min at copy number of 1 copy/µL. However, the results are inconsistent due to Poisson Distribution effect, whereas 10 copies/µL shows intense and steady band. Interestingly at 30 °C (ambient temperature), detection were positive by visual bands; howerver, they were faint band on both test lines. These were too marginal for confident visual interpretation. The HPV-18 signal rose early and then plateaued. The HPV-16 signal remained low until 20 min and then rose steeply. Raising the template from 10 to 100 copies/µL increased the HPV-18 signal and slightly compromised the HPV-16 signal, indicating competition for shared reaction components.

The platform detects both genotypes at 10 copies/µL within 30 min at body temperature without requiring a thermal cycler, power supply, and or readout instrument. It is therefore suited to cervical cancer diagnosis in clinics and community settings where laboratory infrastructure is absent. With further optimization and thorough clinical validation, the MIRA-LFD assay system has the potential to become a promising point-of-care testing platform.

title: Docking and Molecular Dynamics of the Natural Diterpenoid Dihydrotanshinone I in Human 15-PGDH Across Three Inhibitor-Bound Receptor Structures
authors: Sabbir Ahmad Antor, Md Abu Sadat Soash, Muktadir Al Mahmud, Raphael Kabir Niloy, Md. Mainul Hossain Bakul, Gokul Chandra Biswas
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (15-PGDH) is the enzyme that inactivates prostaglandin E2, and its inhibition raises prostaglandin E2 and rejuvenates aged skeletal muscle, which makes it an attractive target for age-related muscle decline. Although natural products are documented functional inhibitors of 15-PGDH, almost none has been characterized by structure-based docking, and the tanshinones of Salvia miltiorrhiza have not been examined against this enzyme. Here, dihydrotanshinone I, with panaxynol as a comparator, was docked into three experimentally determined 15-PGDH structures, the X-ray cocrystals 9PFL and 9PFM and the cryo-electron microscopy structure 8CVN, using a protocol validated for each receptor by redocking its own crystallographic inhibitor (heavy-atom RMSD 0.38 to 1.46 Å).

Dihydrotanshinone I docked favourably into the inhibitor pocket of all three structures, with best predicted docking affinities of −8.94 to −10.5 kcal/mol. In the X-ray structures, it formed a hydrogen bond with catalytic Ser138 and contacted Tyr151 and the lid-hinge residue Phe185, whereas in the cryo-electron microscopy structure it was anchored by Phe185 and Tyr217. Across fifteen independent random seeds the top pose was highly reproducible in every structure, with maximum pairwise RMSDs below 0.2 Å, confirming that it is the dominant docking solution and not a seed-dependent artefact. The precise orientation was only partly conserved across the ensemble, so a single rigid binding mode is not established by docking alone.

Triplicate 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of all three complexes, nine trajectories in total, showed that the compound remained in continuous contact with the protein throughout every run and retained its contacts with the inhibitor-site residues, that Phe185 is contacted in essentially every frame while Lys155 is contacted in none, and that the three docked poses remained largely distinct under receptor flexibility, with one 8CVN replica of nine relocating toward the 9PFL pose. These three results were unchanged when recomputed across equilibration discard windows of 0 to 50 ns. Together the docking and the simulations identify dihydrotanshinone I as a reproducible, mechanistically plausible natural-compound candidate for the 15-PGDH inhibitor pocket. Predicted binding is reported as an estimate of binding potential and not as proven enzyme inhibition.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery: Problems and Prospects - A Case Study in Predictive Modeling and Virtual Screening for Acetylcholinesterase Inhibition
authors: Md Abu Sadat Soash, Sajib Mia
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is frequently described as transformative for drug discovery, yet recent critical appraisals note that its demonstrated clinical impact remains limited relative to the scale of investment and publication in the field. This study examines the problems and prospects of AI in drug discovery through a literature review combined with an original, fully reproducible case study targeting human acetylcholinesterase (AChE)—the biological target of every approved symptomatic Alzheimer's disease therapy.

Using bioactivity data extracted directly from the official ChEMBL release 37 SQLite database for human AChE (CHEMBL220), we built Random Forest models predicting inhibitory potency (pIC50, R² = 0.72, RMSE = 0.74) and active/inactive status (ROC-AUC = 0.966, Accuracy 91.3%) from 1024-bit Morgan circular fingerprints alone. Model validity was verified via 3-fold cross-validation and a rigorous 5-iteration Y-randomization control, which collapsed performance to chance level (R² ≈ -0.19, AUC ≈ 0.50) upon activity label shuffling, definitively ruling out data leakage and artificial inflation.

Interpretability analysis revealed that the model independently rediscovered the canonical O–C(=O)–NH carbamate pharmacophore shared by clinically used AChE inhibitors (rivastigmine, neostigmine, and physostigmine) without prior biochemical supervision. The validated models were then applied to virtually screen 738,823 natural products from the COCONUT database within a defined applicability domain. The pipeline reliably recovered known benchmark inhibitors (donepezil, tacrine, and the physostigmine alkaloid family) while prioritizing a non-duplicate chemotype, 2-butyl-diazaspiro[4,4]non-1-en-4-ones (derived from the irbesartan core intermediate), independently corroborated by published in vitro Ellman enzymatic inhibition literature. Together, these results illustrate both the genuine computational prospects and the practical constraints—data curation burdens, applicability domains, and the essential distinction between rediscovery and true novelty—that characterize contemporary AI-driven drug discovery.

title: Targeting High-Risk Macrophage Phenotypes in the Breast Cancer Microenvironment: A Single-Cell Transcriptomic and Drug Repurposing Analysis
authors: Md Abu Sadat Soash, Raphael Kabir Niloy
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
The tumor microenvironment (TME) is a complex ecosystem where distinct cellular states dictate disease progression and therapeutic resistance. In this study, we performed a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic dissection of the breast cancer TME using publicly available scRNA-seq data (12 paired samples across 6 patients; 98,410 high-quality cells). Unsupervised clustering identified 39 distinct cellular subpopulations. By applying the Single-Cell Phenotype-Associated Signatures (scPAS) risk-scoring algorithm mapped against TCGA-BRCA survival metrics, we discovered a highly immunosuppressive macrophage subpopulation that serves as a primary driver of high-risk clinical phenotypes.

Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that these scPAS+ macrophages are hyper-metabolic, relying heavily on Oxidative Phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and are actively engaged in antigen presentation, phagocytosis, and chemotaxis to orchestrate an immunosuppressive ecosystem. To identify therapeutic vulnerabilities, we deployed dual in silico drug repurposing pipelines (DrugReSC and ASGARD). These analyses consistently identified targeted kinase inhibitors (e.g., Dabrafenib, Vemurafenib, Imatinib, Pazopanib) and proteasome inhibitors (e.g., Ixazomib) as top candidates capable of reversing the high-risk transcriptomic signature. Our findings provide a robust computational framework for identifying and targeting prognostic macrophage states to improve breast cancer immunotherapy outcomes.

title: scRNA-seq Guided In Silico Drug Repurposing Identifies Candidate Therapeutics for Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome lacks targeted FDA-approved therapeutics. This study aims to identify novel therapeutic candidates capable of reversing the pathogenic transcriptomic signatures of HFRS, specifically targeting the abnormal presence of Nucleated Red Blood Cells (NRBCs) and multilineage immune dysregulation.

We obtained peripheral blood mononuclear cell single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from HFRS patients and healthy controls. Utilizing Seurat v5 for data integration and the ASGARD computational pipeline, we extracted differential expression profiles and queried them against the LINCS L1000 pharmacogenomic database.

The multi-cluster ASGARD pipeline successfully identified 13 statistically significant FDA-approved drug candidates. Vorinostat and Tretinoin emerged as the top-ranked candidates capable of rescuing immune hyper-inflammation and HFRS-induced erythroid maturation arrest.

Our in silico framework successfully translates scRNA-seq pathogenesis data into actionable therapeutic targets, providing a strong rationale for immediate in vitro validation of Vorinostat and Tretinoin for HFRS treatment.

title: Host Industrialization Drives Dietary-Dependent Structural Variation and Gene Shedding in the Human Gut Archaeon Methanobrevibacter smithii
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Background: Methanobrevibacter smithii is the dominant archaeal keystone species in the human gut, playing a crucial role in syntrophic hydrogen removal. While bacterial responses to host industrialization and Westernized diets are well documented, the adaptive capacity of the gut archaeome remains largely unexplored due to an over-reliance on 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

Methods: To investigate archaeal structural adaptation, we conducted a pan-metagenomic analysis of 219 high-quality M. smithii Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) retrieved from the UHGG catalog. We stratified the genomes into an Industrialized cohort (US and UK; n=172) and a Non-Industrialized cohort (Peru, Fiji, Madagascar; n=47) to identify lifestyle-specific accessory gene biomarkers.

Results: M. smithii possesses a highly open pangenome, with a massive cloud genome constituting 77.4% of its genetic repertoire. Statistical enrichment analysis revealed a striking pattern of diet-driven gene shedding. Industrialized strains exhibited a near-total loss of genes related to Vitamin B12 scavenging (BtuC/D) and Lysine biosynthesis, reflecting an adaptation to nutrient-dense Western diets. Conversely, industrialized strains showed significant enrichment in methanogenesis optimization genes, notably the polyferredoxin protein MvhB.

Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that M. smithii is not a static monolithic entity but a highly dynamic symbiote. Its accessory genome is actively sculpted by host dietary history and localized ecological pressures, highlighting the necessity of strain-level structural analysis in understanding microbiome evolution.

title: Environmental Resistome and Homogenization of Extremotolerant Communities in Jet Propulsion Laboratory Cleanroom Environments
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) cleanroom environments adhere to strict planetary protection protocols to minimize microbial bioburden, inadvertently creating selective pressures that drive the survival of extremotolerant, multidrug-resistant (MDR) microbes. This study maps the spatial distribution and ecological diversity of the environmental resistome within a JPL Mars Exploration Program cleanroom using short-read metagenomic sequencing data (OSD-944). Following the removal of mock community controls and normalization of sequencing depth to Coverage Per Million (CPM), the resistome was characterized against the KEGG and BacMet databases.

Spatial analysis revealed the highest localized burdens of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in human transition zones, specifically the floor by cabinets (1,211.6 CPM) and gowning rooms (1,066.5 CPM), while critical spacecraft assembly surfaces exhibited near-zero AMR loads. Despite these observational differences, statistical evaluations including Kruskal-Wallis (H = 8.5686, p = 0.285) and PERMANOVA (pseudo-F = 1.123, p = 0.321) indicated no significant spatial variance in total AMR burden or microbial community composition across the facility footprint. Taxonomic profiling identified primary carriers of resistance mechanisms as Acinetobacter, Brevundimonas, and Paracoccus species, alongside eukaryotic fungi such as Aspergillus. The detection of broad-spectrum efflux pumps, such as mexJK, and dual-resistance genes highlights a uniform, highly selected microbiome shaped by stringent sterilization protocols.

title: Comparative Pan-Genomic and Functional Analysis of Shigella Bacteriophages Reveals a Fragmented, Genome Size-Linked Population Structure
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Shigella species are a major cause of bacterial dysentery, with substantial disease burden in Bangladesh and other low- and middle-income countries. Rising antibiotic resistance has renewed interest in bacteriophages as alternative therapeutic agents. However, the genomic diversity and gene content of known Shigella phages have not been systematically characterized, limiting understanding of their suitability for therapeutic development. This study aimed to characterize the pan-genome, functional gene content, and genomic clustering of publicly available complete Shigella phage genomes.

Fifty-four complete Shigella phage genomes were retrieved from the NCBI RefSeq database. Genes were annotated with Pharokka, which assigned functional categories and screened for virulence factors (VFDB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (CARD). Pan-genome composition was determined with Roary, and genomes were grouped by proteomic similarity using PhamClust.

Pan-genome analysis identified 4,321 gene clusters with no core genes shared across all 54 genomes, 206 shell genes, and 4,115 cloud genes. Of 9,040 predicted coding sequences, the largest annotated categories were DNA/RNA metabolism (13.9%) and tail proteins (9.0%), while 54.6% remained unannotated. Two genomes carried gtrA/gtrB/gtr-type serotype-converting genes; no antimicrobial resistance genes were detected. PhamClust grouped genomes into 11 clusters and 13 singletons, with the two largest clusters corresponding to genome size: large phages (165-194 kb, 12 genomes) and small phages (~50 kb, 7 genomes).

Shigella phages form multiple distinct, size-linked lineages rather than one uniform population. The serotype-converting genes reflect known lysogenic conversion mechanisms in Shigella flexneri phages, while the absence of resistance genes supports their suitability for therapeutic exploration. This fragmentation indicates the Shigella phage population lacks a shared core genome, a baseline finding relevant to future cocktail-based phage therapy strategies against Shigella.

title: In Silico Structural and Functional Annotation of Hypothetical Protein ACLVWE_24230 from Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi Plasmid: An MqsA-Family Antitoxin and HTH Transcriptional Regulator
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi is the causative agent of typhoid fever, an invasive systemic disease posing substantial global healthcare challenges. Plasmids within S. enterica frequently harbor genes of unknown biological significance ("hypothetical proteins") that may drive plasmid maintenance, virulence, stress resilience, or antibiotic tolerance. In this research, an extensive, multi-tier in silico workflow was deployed to structurally and functionally annotate the uncharacterized hypothetical protein ACLVWE_24230 (GenBank: XYZ87145.1), encoded on a plasmid of S. enterica serovar Typhi.

Physicochemical profiling characterized ACLVWE_24230 as an 80-amino-acid, basic (theoretical pI = 9.00), hydrophilic (GRAVY = −0.761), and highly stable (Instability Index = 21.18) cytoplasmic protein with a molecular weight of 9.015 kDa. Conserved Domain Database (CDD) and Pfam analyses revealed the presence of a definitive MqsA-family antitoxin domain (pfam15731, E-value: 3.84 × 10⁻⁵) harboring a conserved Helix-Turn-Helix (HTH_XRE) DNA-binding motif (cd00093). High-confidence 3D homology modeling using the AlphaFold-predicted template of YajA from Salmonella thompson achieved full-length sequence coverage with a Global Model Quality Estimation (GMQE) score of 0.90. Stereochemical validation via MolProbity yielded a MolProbity score of 0.92, zero clash score, and 93.59% residues in favored Ramachandran regions. Cavity analysis identified a major functional surface pocket (Area = 134.88 Å², Volume = 250.55 Å³) clustering within the HTH motif. Molecular docking against toxin MqsR (from PDB: 3HI2) via ClusPro demonstrated high-affinity interaction (Cluster 0 weighted score: −720.3 kcal/mol) with an interface backbone RMSD = 0.075 Å relative to experimental E. coli MqsA-MqsR complexes. These findings demonstrate that ACLVWE_24230 functions as an MqsA-family antitoxin and HTH transcriptional regulator, providing insights into plasmid stability and bacterial persistence in typhoid fever.

title: BMPPD: Bangladeshi Medicinal Plant Phytochemicals Database
authors: Sk. Faisal Ahmed, Amir Alve, Imranur Rahman, Abir Hossain, Shormila Akter Sumya, Md Shah Paran, Md Abu Sadat Soash, Md Raihan Ahmed, Esha Mony Bristy, Kaniz Fatema, Md Asif Siddque Jim, Zannatul Firdaus, Rafa Uddin, Md Tajul Islam, Taiyara Mahjabin, Md Ismail Hossain, Rakibul Hasan Alif, Md Aftabur Rahman, Rahat Moinul Islam, Foysal Ahmed, Mst. Marjeya, Mst. Afrin Mustari, Md Ashrarul Hasib, Md Sadique Hossain, Nishat Ulfat Nity, Md Foisal Imtiaz, Ovejan Paul Rudra, Asifuzzaman Zisan, Md Delwar Hossen, Tania Akter Nirjona, Prami Chowdhury Badhan
affiliation: Dawn of Bioinformatics Limited, Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract:
Natural products derived from medicinal flora represent a primary cornerstone of pharmacophore discovery and traditional healthcare systems. Despite Bangladesh's extensive botanical diversity and deep-rooted ethnopharmacological heritage, scientific exploration of these bioresources has historically suffered from fragmented literature, unstandardized vernacular taxonomies, and an absence of unified computational repositories.

Here, we present the Bangladeshi Medicinal Plant Phytochemicals Database (BMPPD) (https://bmppd.org), the first comprehensive, peer-curated, web-accessible cheminformatics and ethnobotanical database devoted to the medicinal plants of Bangladesh. Developed over two years of rigorous literature synthesis at Dawnilab (the research hub of Dawn of Bioinformatics Limited, Dhaka, Bangladesh), BMPPD bridges ethnobotanical folk taxonomy with structured molecular cheminformatics.

Currently, the operational database indexes 341 verified botanical species, linked to 712 vernacular/common names, 31,717 curated plant–metabolite associations, 16,333 unique phytochemical entities, and 10,302 cross-referenced PubChem Compound Identifiers (CIDs), with a cumulative data pipeline encompassing upwards of 700 medicinal taxa and >113,000 phytochemical entries. Equipped with multi-tiered querying (scientific nomenclature, vernacular designations, compound designations, and PubChem CIDs), automated literature provenance tracing, and an interactive crowdsourced plant request tracking mechanism, BMPPD provides an open, high-performance foundation for secondary metabolite exploration, virtual screening, network pharmacology, and rational drug discovery.

title: PhageBiomeLab: Phage Bank Initiative in Bangladesh
developers: Md Abu Sadat Soash, Mutashim Ahammed Rafi
supervisor: Prof. Dr. Md. Shakhinur Islam Mondal
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) represents one of the most critical threats to modern global public health. The PhageBiome Lab conducts in vivo and in silico investigations into bacteriophage therapy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial pathogens, microbiome dynamics, and pathogen genomics.

Microbiology and genomic research wet-labs frequently face challenges with fragmented spreadsheets, loss of historical isolate metadata (e.g., 16S rRNA sequences, host range, storage temperatures), and lack of synchronized public dissemination. To mitigate these challenges, PhageBiomeLab (https://phagebiomelab.com) was developed as a centralized scientific data infrastructure, biobank repository, and academic portal for the PhageBiome Research Group at Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh.

The platform integrates a comprehensive biological repository cataloging bacterial strains (taxonomic markers, isolation sources, AMR susceptibility profiles, and -80°C cryostorage) and a specialized bacteriophage biobank with host-range specificity, lifecycle characteristics, and electron microscopy data. Built on a production-grade Django architecture with relational database governance, automated deployment webhooks, and integrated academic CV tracking, PhageBiomeLab provides a structured, scalable digital ecosystem for phage research and biocontrol initiatives.

title: Epidemiological and Clinical Case Study on Clubfoot (CTEV) in Bangladesh
authors: Md Nehamul Islam Nehad, Sunayda Jahan Sruty, Ridoy Chandra Roy, Md Abu Sadat Soash, Shatabdi Roy, Alvee Alam, Jahidul Islam Shovo, Shadman Mutassim Efad
affiliation: Department of Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, Sylhet, Bangladesh
abstract:
Clubfoot is a congenital foot deformity characterised by medial deviation of the heel, forefoot adduction, and ankle inversion. While global prevalence is approximately 1 in 1,000 live births, in Bangladesh the estimated incidence is around 1 in 900 births (~5,000 children born each year with the condition).

This study documents primary clinical, familial, and demographic profiles of 16 patients evaluated through hospital visits and door-to-door field interviews across multiple districts of Bangladesh. The investigation assesses:
• Clinical variation and deformity classification (Equinovarus, Varus, unilateral vs. bilateral).
• Therapeutic interventions (the non-invasive Ponseti method involving serial casting, Achilles tenotomy, and bracing vs. surgical procedures).
• Potential hereditary components and syndromic associations (chromosomal involvement such as 17q23 microdeletions/duplications, trisomies, and multi-generational recurrence).
• Socioeconomic bottlenecks, healthcare infrastructure gaps, and treatment adherence barriers affecting low-income families in Bangladesh.
